The soft hum of the television filled the quiet room, an idle soundtrack to Mydei’s restless mind. The faint glow from the screen illuminated the cluttered apartment—empty coffee mugs stacked haphazardly, a half-open book on the couch beside him, and the ever-present reminder of his new reality: a knee brace that sat beside him like an unwanted companion.

It was an early afternoon, but Mydei hadn’t bothered to leave his couch. There was no need to. He didn’t have a schedule anymore—no early morning runs, no tight training regimens, no match preparations. All that was gone, replaced by the monotonous routines of a life that no longer felt his own. The pain in his knee had become a constant, an ache that settled into his bones, no matter how still he was. He tried to ignore it as best he could, but some days it was louder than others.

The game on the television was nothing new, just another replay of one of Phainon’s recent matches. The familiar faces of players, the aggressive tackles, the beautiful fluid passes—he had lived it. He had been it. The fast-paced action of soccer, the sharp focus, the brutal intensity, all of it had once been his world. The crowd’s roar, the energy that pulsed through him as he sprinted across the pitch—it had been so effortless back then.

But that was before the injury.

He turned his eyes away from the screen, letting the pictures blur as he closed them for a moment. It wasn’t the game that consumed him now, not anymore. It was the memory—the sudden, sharp moment when everything changed. That one instant had led him down an entirely different path.

It was late in the first half of the match. His team was pushing forward, the ball coming to him in a fast break. He was poised to make his signature move—a sharp cut to the left, followed by a cross to his forward, setting up a perfect chance to score. But as his foot planted, as he began to push off the turf to make the turn, he felt it. A sharp, sickening snap. The world seemed to freeze for a moment, the sound of it echoing in his ears.

The pain hit him a second later—blinding, all-consuming. His knee buckled beneath him, sending him crashing to the ground, his body contorting in ways it shouldn’t have. He couldn’t breathe, couldn’t focus on anything except the overwhelming agony that shot through his leg. Every movement felt like it was fighting against him, like his body was betraying him in the most unforgiving way.

He could still hear the trainer’s voice, the panic in it, the urgency. The next few minutes blurred into an unrecognizable mess of voices and movement. The crowd’s cheers turned to confused murmurs, the stadium atmosphere shifting as Mydei was helped off the field. He couldn’t even remember getting to the locker room, only the stark white of the lights and the pressure of hands on his leg, trying to stabilize it.

The tests, the scans, the long days of waiting, all felt like part of a different life. The diagnosis was the one thing that would change everything: Severe ACL tear. Chronic instability. Full recovery is unlikely. It didn’t matter how much therapy he went through, or how hard he worked to get back to the game. His knee would never be the same.

In those early days after the injury, Mydei had refused to believe it. He’d ignored the doctor’s words, even as his body told him otherwise. He’d worked through the pain, pushing harder than he ever had, telling himself it was just temporary, that he would come back stronger. He had been so determined, so focused on returning to his former glory that the reality of what was happening didn’t truly sink in.

It wasn’t until months later, during one of his rehab sessions, when he tried to take a step—just a step—and his knee gave out again that the finality of it hit him. The pang of disappointment. The heavyweight of resignation. It was at that moment that he knew: This was it. This was all I have now.

The hardest part hadn’t been the physical pain, though. It had been the knowledge that his career, his entire identity, was tied to that one injury. The thought that he would never play again, never feel the rush of a game, never compete in front of a roaring crowd—those were the things that had broken him. Not the pain, not the endless days in rehab, but the loss of himself.

It wasn’t long before the media had spun their narrative—retirement due to injury, sure, but the rumors swirled. They couldn’t resist turning it into something more salacious. They had painted him as a has-been , washed up and left behind by the sport that had defined him. They said he was weak. They said he didn’t have the grit to fight through it. It wasn’t just the press that hurt him, though—it was the way the world had moved on without him. His friends had moved on. His teammates, former rivals, and even Phainon had moved on.

But not Phainon. Phainon had stayed.

Even when the calls from his teammates stopped coming, even when the invitations to “grab a drink” stopped, Phainon kept reaching out. It wasn’t often, but it was consistent. He never let Mydei feel entirely forgotten. Phainon sent the occasional text, checked in, and asked how the rehab was going. It wasn’t much, but it was enough to remind Mydei that he wasn’t completely alone.

And even though it wasn’t much, there was always the reminder of Phainon’s brilliance in the sport—his name plastered across billboards, magazine covers, and endless headlines. The media’s sweetheart. The golden boy. Phainon was a professional who could do no wrong. Winning title after title, his natural talent and drive make him an unstoppable force on the field. It was a game of jet-setting for him now, traveling country to country, competing in the biggest leagues, always in the spotlight.

The last time Mydei had seen Phainon in person had been at the championship game—a competition that had been the talk of the year. Phainon’s team had won the prestigious Copa de la Liga , a major international championship, with Phainon scoring the winning goal in the final match. It had been a spectacular moment for Phainon, a moment of glory that only seemed to add to his already massive reputation.

The headlines had been everywhere— Phainon’s Victory Secures Another Title —and the way the world had celebrated him only reminded Mydei of everything he had lost. But he couldn’t be angry. He couldn’t bring himself to resent Phainon for it. Phainon deserved every accolade and every recognition that came his way. He had worked for it, and Mydei wouldn’t begrudge him that.

But damn, the stabbing feeling still lingered when he saw Phainon’s face in those headlines, winning another title while Mydei was left behind in the shadows.

As Phainon’s name filled the screen for another highlight, Mydei caught himself thinking about the distance between them, the rare times they managed to see each other. Phainon was always on the move—always chasing the next game, the next title. It made sense, but it didn’t make the space any easier to bear.

He’s just doing his job , Mydei reminded himself, quickly pushing the thought away. He has a life, just like I have mine now.

It had been years since the injury, but sometimes it felt like it had only happened yesterday.

The room felt a little quieter now, the hum of the TV almost like background noise as Mydei scrolled idly through his phone. He didn’t expect to see anything new, just the usual assortment of headlines—sports gossip, random fan photos, and the occasional interview. But one headline caught his attention.

The picture beside it was one he recognized immediately: Phainon, grinning like the sun itself had exploded in his chest, lifting Cyrene into the air after winning the Copa de la Liga finals. Her laughter was infectious, her face framed by the light of the stadium’s floodlights, eyes sparkling as Phainon spun her around. She was always so full of warmth, so kind, so effortless in her joy.

The headline read: Phainon Celebrates Championship Win with Special Guest Cyrene—A Bond Stronger Than the Game?

Mydei let out a breath he hadn’t realized he’d been holding. He couldn’t help but smile at the picture, even though it dug at something deep in his chest. They were perfect for each other, weren’t they?

Cyrene wasn’t like the others, the people who hovered around Phainon in the media, desperate for a piece of his spotlight. She was genuine, unpretentious—one of the few people who had always treated him with kindness, even when the world around him was spinning out of control. Mydei had seen it in the way she interacted with Phainon: the subtle touches, the way her eyes softened when she looked at him, the way they could speak without words. It was the kind of connection he had always envied, the kind of relationship he could only wish for.

And yet…

There was still the weird, inexplicable bond he shared with Phainon, the one that had existed long before Cyrene had come into the picture. It wasn’t exactly a friendship—at least not the kind they had once shared when they were on the same team. It wasn’t a rivalry either, not anymore. It was something…in between. Something that lived in the gray area of what they used to have and what they could be now, in this strange situation they’d found themselves in.

Mydei was ashamed to admit it, but he was selfish about it. He didn’t want to let it go, even though he knew he probably should. He wasn’t sure when it had started, this something between him and Phainon, but it had always felt so easy when they were together. It was almost like picking up where they left off, no matter how much time had passed.

Maybe that was the problem.

Phainon had moved on—his world was Cyrene now, his victories, his life. And Mydei was just left in the periphery, still clinging to whatever was left of their past. But he wasn’t ready to let it go. Not yet. Not when it still felt like there was something there , even if it was just the echoes of their old friendship, the faintest hint of something more.

But no. Mydei quickly banished that thought. He couldn’t be selfish. Not with someone like Cyrene in Phainon’s life. She was good for him. She made him happy. And Phainon deserved that happiness, no matter how bittersweet it was for Mydei.

Still, the ache in his chest didn’t go away, even as he kept his eyes glued to the photo of Phainon and Cyrene, laughing and spinning in each other’s arms.

Maybe one day, Mydei thought, he’ll see me the way he sees her. But not now. Not yet.

He immediately cut that line of thought off. He couldn’t be thinking like this, not anymore. Not when the truth was painfully clear—Phainon was never going to see him that way. He’d had his chances, hadn’t he? Their moments, the lingering touches, the way they’d always been able to talk for hours about nothing at all—those were just the comfortable rhythms of an old friendship, nothing more. Nothing that should’ve meant anything more.

He needed to let go of this. The moments when their fingers brushed against each other on accident, the times Phainon had leaned just a little too close when speaking to him, the occasional late-night phone calls where Phainon’s voice would slip into something softer, more intimate—those things didn’t mean anything. Not really.

And yet, every time Phainon would smile at him, that warmth would flood Mydei’s chest. It would feel like something more like he was the one Phainon was letting in—letting closer, even when it was obvious that no one else would. There were times, small moments in between when Mydei could swear there was something there. A glance that lingered a second too long, an unspoken understanding when they didn’t need to say a word. He thought maybe—just maybe—he was special to Phainon in some way that no one else was.

But no. He couldn’t let himself get carried away with that idea. Phainon had Cyrene now. He was happy. He deserved that. Mydei was selfish for even hoping that this—whatever this was between them—could be more than it ever would be.

Still, when Phainon’s name popped up on his phone screen, a part of him couldn’t help the way his heart quickened, the way his thumb hovered for a second too long before he answered. They spoke often, more often than Mydei was ready to admit. There were times when their conversations would flow seamlessly, their easy rapport making it feel like nothing had changed. Phainon would ask about his day, about the injury, about how he was feeling—sometimes with an easy, casual tone, sometimes with something softer, something that felt like concern.

It was moments like those that Mydei found himself reaching for his phone even when he knew he shouldn’t, moments where he felt like he was holding onto a thread that would unravel if he let go. Phainon had been there when Mydei was struggling, long after the injury ended his career. He’d visited and helped him through the worst days. Mydei would never forget that. But there was always that lingering distance now, that invisible line between them that neither of them ever seemed willing to cross.

It wasn’t that Phainon was indifferent—far from it. He had a way of making Mydei feel like he mattered like he was still important. But it was the way Phainon was with Cyrene that always left a bitter taste in his mouth. He was different from her, in a way that Mydei couldn’t ignore. There was an ease to it, an openness, a depth that Mydei could never seem to replicate. The way Phainon would lean into her touch, the way he’d smile at her as though the rest of the world faded away when she was around.

I’m not jealous, Mydei repeated to himself, trying to quell the unease that churned in his stomach. I’m not jealous. But damn it, he couldn’t help it. He wasn’t just watching Phainon from the sidelines anymore. He was watching him from the edge of something he couldn’t quite define—half-friend, half-something else—while Cyrene had the full version of him. And that… that was hard to swallow.

Yet here he was, clinging to the little moments they still had. The texts, the calls, the quiet, unspoken understanding. He wanted to be content with that, to let go of these feelings that were too tangled to sort out. But every time Phainon’s name lit up his phone screen, or when he would hear Phainon’s voice just a little too close, Mydei felt that pull. That hope. That little spark that made him want to believe in something more.

The worst part was, he wasn’t sure if Phainon even realized what he was doing. Did Phainon know the effect he had on him? Or was this all just some unintentional flirtation in the form of friendship that Mydei was reading into too much? He couldn’t know for sure, and that was the hardest part.

But one thing was for certain—he couldn’t keep pretending that the pain in his chest was going to go away on its own. He couldn’t keep pretending that watching Phainon and Cyrene together didn’t tear at something deep inside him.

Mydei couldn’t keep watching them. Phainon and Cyrene, were always so effortless in their affection, so open with their smiles, their touches, the way they seemed to have no reservations in their connection. It made his stomach twist. His hands, once steady and calm, were now clenched into fists at his sides, his chest tight with something he didn’t know how to name.

He wanted Phainon to be happy, wanted him to find the kind of love and peace that was so obvious between him and Cyrene. That was the truth, wasn’t it? It was easy to say that to himself, easy to repeat. He wasn’t jealous, he wasn’t bitter… but in moments like this, when Phainon would pull Cyrene close, smile at her with that look in his eyes that Mydei had never once received, the ache would come back tenfold. He couldn’t deny it any longer.

It wasn’t just about wanting Phainon to be happy. It was about wanting Phainon to notice him. To see him. To see him in the way he needed . Mydei wanted to believe that, deep down, there was something there, something he wasn’t imagining. But whenever he watched Phainon and Cyrene together, he felt like an outsider in his own heart. He wasn’t even sure what he was any more in Phainon’s life—was he a friend? A companion? A distant memory of someone Phainon used to rely on? The more he saw, the more he began to feel like a shadow in the periphery, someone who didn’t belong in the world Phainon had built around himself.

A frustrated, low growl slipped from Mydei’s throat, and he slammed both his hands down on the table in front of him. He couldn’t sit here anymore. He couldn’t keep doing this to himself, letting his emotions spiral, letting his mind run wild over things he couldn’t control.

He needed to get out.

Without giving himself another moment to think, Mydei stood up abruptly, his chair scraping loudly across the floor. His legs felt stiff as he moved, his body protesting the sudden movement, but he ignored it. He grabbed his jacket, yanking it on over his shoulders before heading toward the door.

It wasn’t the first time he’d done this—walked out to clear his head, trying to escape the rising frustration inside him. But this time felt different. The weight of the past few years was heavier today, pressing down on him more than usual.

Once outside, he inhaled deeply, trying to breathe through the knot in his chest. The city around him was still bustling, people going about their lives, completely unaware of the turmoil inside him. And that was fine. That’s how it should be now. Nobody cared about Mydei anymore. He wasn’t the golden boy of soccer, the one everyone wanted to see, the one everyone talked about. Now, he was just another face in the crowd.

At first, that felt like a relief—no more cameras in his face, no more invasive questions about his injury, no more false sympathy from reporters trying to catch him at his lowest. He was just… normal. And for the most part, he appreciated that. The quiet, the anonymity—it was a kind of peace. But now and then, the absence of the spotlight stung. There were moments when he missed being on the field, the adrenaline of the game, the thrill of the crowd cheering his name. But more than that, he missed feeling important, missed the sense of purpose that had driven him through his career.

Now, all he had was the nagging reminder of what he used to be—what he could’ve been, if not for that one fateful moment, that one snap that had changed everything.

Mydei rubbed his eyes, exhaling slowly, trying to shake off the feeling. He didn’t have time for this right now. He needed to focus on something, anything else. His body might’ve healed physically, but the injury lingered in other ways. In the quiet moments of his life, it crept in. He could feel it in the stiffness of his knee every time he moved too quickly, the constant gnawing of it that would flare up when he stood for too long.

It had been years since the ACL tear, and Mydei had mostly gotten used to the dull pain, the way it reminded him of what he’d lost. There were days when it wasn’t as bad, days when he could walk without thinking about it, but there were also days when he felt the weight of it in every step. Days when his knee locked up unexpectedly, forcing him to stop whatever he was doing just to wait for it to loosen again.

And no matter how many times he tried to ignore it, it was there. It was always there.

There was no escaping it—not even in his day-to-day life. Sometimes, when he was walking down the street, just trying to get from one place to another, he could feel people staring. Not in the way they used to, when they were fascinated by his skill or his star power. Now, it was pitying stares. The looks that lingered just a second too long when they noticed the slight limp in his step. Mydei hated it, hated the reminder that he was no longer the athlete he used to be.

But what could he do? The injury had changed everything, and now, all he could do was keep moving forward.

Just keep moving forward, he repeated to himself, taking a slow breath.

He didn’t have Phainon’s success, didn’t have the trophies or the fame. But he still had his own life. And that had to be enough.

He didn’t have Phainon’s life, didn’t have the things that seemed to come so easily to him—relationships, purpose, the certainty of his place in the world. But he still had his own life, even if it felt like a shadow of what it once could’ve been. And for now, that would have to be enough.

Mydei walked into the coffee shop, the familiar jingle of the doorbell above his head a soft reminder that, despite everything, life still moved forward, unbothered. He ordered his coffee quickly—black, nothing special—and found a seat near the window, his body feeling a little more heavy than usual.

The familiar ache in his knee was there, just under the surface, lurking like a quiet reminder that it was always going to be part of him now. He shifted his weight, trying to ease the discomfort that flared up whenever he’d been standing too long. Years of physical therapy had given him back some of what he’d lost, but no amount of time or exercise could fully erase the damage. He knew his limits now—knew the exact moment when he’d push too far and his knee would retaliate.

As he sat down, he shifted his leg carefully, keeping it at an angle that minimized the strain. His right knee had never quite been the same. It wasn’t just the pain anymore—it was the instability. His leg didn’t always feel secure when he walked, a strange sense that it could give out if he wasn’t careful. It was more of a dull, persistent discomfort now, like a reminder that his body had been changed forever.

Even after all the therapy, the strengthening exercises, and the months spent working to get back to some semblance of normal, there were still days when the hurt would rear its head. Some mornings, getting out of bed felt like lifting weights instead of just his legs. Some steps still caused his knee to lock up unexpectedly, forcing him to pause and breathe through the shock of it. He hated that, hated how it could still stop him in his tracks.

But now, it wasn’t as jarring. It had become part of the background noise of his life, the constant hum of his injury, the thing that reminded him that he wasn’t the person he used to be. And though he hated it, he also didn’t know what else to do. It was just a fact. A part of him. It had been years, and he still couldn’t quite accept it.

Mydei leaned back in his chair, sighing, trying to ignore the slow throb that spread up his leg. He had gotten used to this. Used to the adjustments. But still, in moments like this—when the stillness of the coffee shop surrounded him, and he had time to think—his mind wandered.

He wouldn’t be able to play again. That was the reality. No more matches, no more late-night training sessions, no more feeling the ball beneath his feet as he slid across the field, muscles working in harmony. All of that was gone, and no amount of physical therapy or medication would bring it back.

For a second, he wondered if that part of his life would ever really leave him. Would he always miss it? Would he always feel the gap where soccer used to be? Well whatever he felt, it wouldn’t matter anymore.

Mydei took a sip of his coffee, the bitter warmth easing the ache in his chest more than the pain in his leg. He pulled his phone out, scrolling absently through the screen to check his schedule.

A few emails from old teammates, one or two from the physical therapy clinic he still visited on occasion, even though the need for it was less frequent now. He had his regular check-in appointments, routine follow-ups, and the occasional guest appearance for a charity game or soccer camp. But none of that took up much of his time anymore, not compared to the career he used to have.

He was a coach now. Part-time, more or less. He had taken on a few younger players in a local academy, helping them with drills, refining their technique, and guiding them through the mental game of soccer. It wasn’t the thrill of competition, but it was fulfilling in its way. He enjoyed the coaching, the way he could still teach the things he’d learned over the years, even if he couldn’t demonstrate them like he used to.

His day off today meant he didn’t have to worry about the kids or any of the academy’s morning sessions. It was a rare day where he had some time to himself, where he wasn’t running between appointments or putting on a smile for cameras. The quiet felt almost too spacious at times, like the echo of a life that used to be busier, more full of noise.

Still, he liked this routine—enough to make it his own. He glanced at the calendar again, noting a few calls he needed to make later, some paperwork for the academy that had been left undone, and maybe a trip to the gym to keep his leg strong. The gym was where he still found a lot of his focus, even if it was more about managing his injury now than it had ever been about strength. The mirror in front of him reminded him of that every time he stepped onto the treadmill or took up some light weights.

Checking his phone, he saw a text from his assistant at the academy, a reminder about an upcoming youth match he had to attend next weekend. Mydei typed back a quick acknowledgment, then set his phone down with a sigh. The rest of his day? It would be filled with random errands, a little bit of solitude, and maybe even some aimless wandering through town.

A life not bad. But still—empty in some ways.

Mydei glanced out the window, watching the pedestrians pass by as the wind ruffled the leaves of nearby trees. The world still turned outside his bubble, moving on as it always did. He envied the ease with which people moved through their day, unaware of the weight of the past on his shoulders.

His gaze flickered to the corner of the shop where an older couple sat, holding hands, talking softly. His thoughts wandered back, just for a moment, to Phainon—how he’d always carried such effortless grace, whether he was on the field or off it.

But Mydei quickly shook his head, forcing the thoughts away.

He had enough to focus on. And at least today, it was his own life he could control, even if it wasn’t exactly what he had imagined.

He could practically track his movements by the headlines that seemed to follow him everywhere— constant updates about his next match, the interviews, the fans, the endless demands from the media. Phainon was a star in every sense of the word, his face plastered on billboards, his name synonymous with success in every country he played.

Phainon had become the face of global soccer, his feet carrying him across continents, winning titles, and breaking records. Every new trophy added to his collection felt like a subtle reminder of the distance between them—how far Phainon had gone and how firmly Mydei had been left behind.

He could see the joy in Phainon’s eyes in every photo. It was the kind of happiness that was almost tangible, and Mydei couldn’t deny how much he wished he could be a part of that world again. But even if he was, it wouldn’t be the same. Phainon had Cyrene now, and that bond was stronger than anything Mydei could offer.

The envy stung, but he knew better than to dwell on it. He didn’t want to be that person, the one who still pined for something that wasn’t there anymore. Phainon was moving forward, and Mydei had to do the same. But it wasn’t always that easy.

Even now, as he sat in the coffee shop, Phainon’s latest match played in his mind. He had seen the postgame interview—a brief, distracted moment where Phainon was asked about his performance. Phainon had answered with his usual modesty, never one to revel in personal praise, but the glint in his eyes was unmistakable. He was at the top of his game, and that alone should have been enough. It had to be.

Still, Mydei couldn’t help but feel a quiet pounding every time he saw Phainon celebrate another victory. There was something about it— something about how effortlessly Phainon seemed to command the field, how everything seemed to come so naturally for him. It was hard not to think that maybe, if he were still playing, he could have been right there with Phainon, lifting those trophies, feeling the rush of victory together.

But that wasn’t his reality anymore.

Instead, he kept a distance, scrolling past most of the posts about Phainon’s travels or the endless streams of highlights. But even that couldn’t stop the way his heart clenched whenever he’d catch glimpses of his former teammate’s success.

He saw Phainon’s name pop up again—another championship. Another trophy. Another win for the history books. It felt like a constant reminder of what could have been, the person he might still be if things had gone differently.

Maybe Phainon didn’t need him anymore. Maybe he didn’t even want to be reminded of what they once had.

But Mydei couldn’t shake the thought. Mydei’s eyes narrowed slightly as he instinctively stepped aside, but then, in a sudden misstep, her foot caught on the uneven pavement.

Without thinking, his arms shot out to steady her, just as she started to lose her balance. His ankle screamed in protest, a sharp, familiar pain shooting up his leg, but he ignored it, focusing on catching her before she fell.

The girl stumbled, and Mydei instinctively held her up, feeling her weight for just a second before he helped her steady herself.

She blinked, looking up in surprise—and then Mydei froze.

For a moment, all he could do was stare. The girl in his arms was none other than Cyrene. The hoodie, the careful steps—she was hiding from something, from someone, but here she was, right in front of him, after all this time.

“Cyrene?” Mydei’s voice caught in his throat, and he quickly pulled his hands away, stepping back awkwardly.

She looked up at him, her expression melting into something familiar— wide eyes, a hint of surprise, and then a smile. “Mydei?” Her voice was full of warmth, and the way she said his name made everything seem a little less heavy like time had somehow skipped over all the awkwardness and tension.

A burst of emotion hit Mydei. Guilt, mostly. How long had it been since they last saw each other? He had kept his distance, kept to himself, his insecurities turning into a wall between him and everyone. And now, here she was—someone who had always been there, even when he hadn’t wanted to admit it.

“It’s… it’s been a while,” Mydei finally managed, his voice a little rougher than he intended. He tried to force a smile but felt it fall flat.

Cyrene’s smile never wavered. “It has. I’m happy to see you, though. How are you? Still up to your usual things?” She asked the question casually, as though there hadn’t been any distance between them, as if no time had passed.

Mydei hesitated for a moment before answering. “I’m… good. Better than before,” he muttered, his mind flicking back to his knee, the reminders of everything he used to be. “You?”

She tilted her head, clearly sensing something unspoken in his tone, but she didn’t push. “I’m great. But I didn’t expect to run into you here of all places. Fancy seeing you in New York!”

Mydei was silent for a moment, a wave of guilt pressing against his chest. His mind flashed to those times—times he should have reached out, should have been better to her. Instead, he’d let jealousy of her relationship with Phainon cloud his thoughts. What the hell had he been doing?

Cyrene caught his eye, her smile gentle, her tone unaffected by the years of distance between them. “You know,” she said, lowering her hood slightly, “I’m glad you’re still around, Mydei. Glad.” She didn’t say it like she was trying to make him feel better; she just meant it, and somehow, that made everything inside him feel a little lighter.

A heavy sigh slipped past Mydei’s lips. He wasn’t sure why he had felt the need to push everyone away all this time. With Cyrene, it felt like there was no need for any of the walls he’d built up.

“Phainon and I were just talking about you the other day,” she added casually, unaware of the way her words caused Mydei’s chest to tighten. He couldn’t help it, but hearing that brought all his old insecurities to the surface again.

He opened his mouth to say something, but the words didn’t come out right. Instead, he found himself muttering, “I should have… I should’ve reached out sooner.”

Cyrene’s smile softened, and she placed a hand on his shoulder, squeezing gently. “It’s alright. Things happen. We’re here now, though. And I’m glad you’re still here.”

Mydei’s heart twisted. How had he ever let jealousy cloud things with her? Cyrene was nothing but kind, and here he was, worried about things that didn’t matter. Maybe it wasn’t too late to start being better.

“Let’s get some coffee,” Cyrene said, her voice light. “I could use the company.”

Mydei hesitated, his internal conflict still fresh in his mind, but her genuine kindness won out. “Yeah, okay. Let’s go.”

After they ordered their coffee, Cyrene led them to a small corner table in the café, the quiet hum of conversation in the background a nice contrast to the frantic energy of the city outside. Mydei took a sip of his drink, the warmth spreading through him, and felt a strange sense of peace as they sat there.

It had been a while since he’d felt so comfortable in someone else’s company. The conversation was easy—and lighthearted. They talked about old memories from when they’d played together, Cyrene’s latest training routines, and even a bit about Phainon, though Mydei kept his answers vague, trying not to let his discomfort show.

Cyrene smiled, leaning back in her seat. “You’re looking good, Mydei. Really. I didn’t expect to see you looking so… well, at peace.” Her eyes twinkled, and Mydei could see the genuine warmth in her expression, a kindness he hadn’t realized he’d missed so much.

He shrugged, trying not to let himself feel too seen. “I’ve been keeping busy,” he said simply, avoiding the weight of the words he’d wanted to say. He didn’t want to get into the details of his injury or how he’d been holding himself together. There was no need. Not with Cyrene.

He glanced at his phone, to which Cyrene had given him a charger for when they’d got here, remembering that he hadn’t responded to Phainon’s messages yet. He’d promised to let him know when he arrived, and somehow—somehow—he had forgotten. It wasn’t like Phainon would expect much, but Mydei knew the small gestures mattered.

He reached for his phone, tapping on it absentmindedly as he kept up the conversation. Cyrene was recounting a funny moment from a match she’d been in, but Mydei’s mind was elsewhere. His thumb swiped over the screen to Phainon’s message, but before he could reply, his gaze landed on the time.

It was already late. And then, something else caught his attention. His hotel.

His stomach dropped.

He had asked for just one night. One. And that was it. The system had auto-checked him out earlier in the day.

“What the hell?” Mydei muttered under his breath, suddenly feeling a knot tighten in his chest. He could feel the panic beginning to creep in, but he didn’t let it show. Not to Cyrene.

“Everything okay?” Cyrene asked, her voice soft with concern, noticing his shift in demeanor.

“Yeah, yeah,” Mydei said, a little too quickly. “Just… forgot to message Phainon. You know how it is.”

Cyrene didn’t press, letting him off the hook with just a smile. “I’m sure he’ll understand. You’ll catch up later.”

“Yeah,” Mydei murmured, clicking his tongue as he set the phone down, trying to focus on the conversation again. But his mind was still on the hotel situation. He had to figure something out fast, without putting too much strain on his leg.

His phone buzzed in his pocket, and he glanced at it quickly to see an alert about the hotel checkout. No help there.

In his head, he was already running through options: call a car, drag his ass across the city to the hotel to grab his things, then find another place, probably at the last minute, in the chaos of New York. Or he could find something local… something closer… but the thought of navigating that with his leg, his exhaustion, made him groan quietly.

He shoved the worry to the back of his mind for the moment, focusing on Cyrene as she rambled on about one of the team’s recruits. It felt good to leave the stress behind for a few minutes. She always had a way of making things seem lighter, even if it was just for a little while. There was no use in making things worse.

After Cyrene excused herself and headed off to her next task, Mydei took a moment to collect his things. His bag slung over his shoulder, he mentally prepared himself for the next step—finding somewhere to stay. But when he started checking hotels, a sinking realization hit him.

Every place in the city was overbooked. It seemed like the whole world had descended on New York to watch the game. No surprise, considering Phainon’s star power. Mydei, too stubborn to give up, tried to look for alternatives, but time passed, and the search seemed endless. Eventually, defeated, he dropped his bag down on the nearest bench, rubbing his temples. What the hell was he even doing here?

With a sigh, he fished out his phone, mindlessly scrolling. The streets of New York were as busy as ever, and his thoughts were heavy, his stomach an odd mix of excitement and dread. Amid his thoughts, he hesitated for a moment, then decided to do something he hadn’t in a while: he called Phainon.

It rang a few times before Phainon’s voice finally came through, sounding lighter than Mydei expected, as though the chaos of the game hadn’t caught up to him just yet.

“Look who’s calling. I figured you’d finally cave and reach out,” Phainon said with a teasing tone.

Mydei couldn’t help but roll his eyes, though a slight grin tugged at the corner of his lips. “I needed something to distract me. Seems like I’ve got plenty of time to kill in this damn city.”

Phainon chuckled. “I hear that. New York’s got a way of swallowing people whole. What’s up?”

“Just… trying to get a grip on this place.” Mydei shrugged, even though Phainon couldn’t see it. “Everything’s either packed or overpriced. Not much room left for me.”

“Sounds like fun,” Phainon teased. “Well, you could’ve booked a room with me. I told you before—I’ve got a whole hotel suite with space to spare.”

“Don’t think you’re getting off that easy,” Mydei said flatly. “I don’t need to sleep next to your ego.”

“Now, that’s cold. I could’ve given you the best bed in the place.” Phainon chuckled again, but there was something softer behind it. “You sure you’re alright though? I know traveling’s not exactly easy on you.”

“I’m fine,” Mydei said, his voice steady. “Just tired, that’s all.”

“Yeah, I bet. So, what’s the plan for tonight?” Phainon asked. “Found a spot yet? Or just sitting in some random corner like you always do?”

Mydei raised an eyebrow, though no one could see him. “Not exactly, but close enough.”

“Should’ve let me know when you were coming. I would’ve made time for you,” Phainon said lightly, and there was something in his tone that made Mydei’s heart skip a beat.

It took him a second to respond, words caught in his throat. His gaze drifted to the streetlights as he forced a nonchalant tone. “Well, I’m just here for the game, not to bother you.”

Phainon laughed, and it was just the right sound, warm and sincere. “You wouldn’t be bothering me. I’m serious. You should’ve let me know.”

Mydei felt his chest tighten. It was too easy to get lost in the sound of Phainon’s voice, but he quickly caught himself before he said anything too revealing. Instead, he shifted the conversation. “I ran into Cyrene today. It’s been a while since I saw her.”

“Oh?” Phainon’s voice was curious, surprised. “How’d that go?”

“It was fine,” Mydei said quickly. “She’s… good. I bumped into her on the street.”

Phainon seemed amused by the way Mydei phrased it. “Well, I’m glad you’re both doing okay. I’ve been hearing a lot about her lately.”

Mydei stayed quiet for a moment, feeling the weight of the conversation settle in. “Yeah,” he muttered, forcing the words out. “I should get going though.”

“Alright,” Phainon replied, his voice soft but teasing. “You better not be running off to avoid me. But hey, if you’re in the area tomorrow, let me know. We can catch up for real”

“No promises,” Mydei said with a smirk in his voice, his heart rate picking up somewhat.

They exchanged a few more words, light banter before the conversation came to an end. Mydei hung up, his thoughts still swirling around the call.

He didn’t even notice the rain until it started to hit his face, the cool droplets a sharp contrast to the warmth of the conversation. He sat there for a while longer, watching the rain blur the streetlights.

A small sigh left him. Maybe things weren’t as complicated as they seemed, but his heart still ached in a way he couldn’t shake.

The rain made everything harder. The wet pavement was slick beneath Mydei’s steps, and he had to slow down, forcing himself to plant his foot carefully with each movement. His knee had never been forgiving in conditions like this, the instability making itself known with every uneven surface.

A group of people hurried past him, their steps quick and sure, and he clenched his jaw, irritated at how easily they moved while he had to think about every step. The cold only made it worse. His knee was in bad shape, the familiar dull throb settling deep into the joint, but he ignored it, tightening his grip on the strap of his bag.

He just needed to get back.

The city lights reflected off the rain-slicked streets, everything blurring together in a haze of gold and red. He pushed forward, stepping onto a curb a little too fast. His knee buckled slightly, and he caught himself before he could stumble, sucking in a sharp breath through his nose.

He exhaled slowly. Kept moving.

A couple under a shared umbrella passed by, the woman casting him a glance. Maybe she noticed the slight hitch in his step, or maybe he just looked as tired as he felt. Either way, Mydei didn’t meet her gaze. He had nothing to say.

The rain wasn’t letting up. His clothes were damp, his muscles tense from the cold, and the hotel situation was still unresolved. He sighed, rubbing a hand down his face. His phone was charged now—he could start looking for another place to stay, but the idea of moving around more, of dealing with the hassle of check-ins and crowded lobbies, made him want to sit down right where he stood.

His fingers flexed at his side. The conversation with Phainon still lingered in his mind, overlapping with the steady pattern of rain.

Maybe, for just a moment, he could stop thinking.

He spotted a bench nearby, mostly dry under the awning of a closed shop. With one last glance around, he made his way over and sat down, stretching his leg out slightly. His knee twinged in protest, but he ignored it, leaning his head back against the wall.

For now, he’d just sit. Just for a little while.

Mydei sat there for longer than he intended, rain tapping against the awning above him, cold settling deep into his limbs. His phone rested in his palm, his thumb hovering over the screen. He could start looking for another hotel —see if something had opened up, try his luck again—but the thought alone exhausted him. His knee was stiff, the soreness settling in stubbornly, and if he was being honest with himself, the idea of wandering the city any longer was out of the question.

His gaze flicked to his call log.

You should’ve let me know when you were coming. I would’ve made time for you.

Mydei exhaled sharply through his nose.

This was stupid. He could find another place. He didn’t need to rely on Phainon. He didn’t need to take the easy way out, even if every logical part of him knew this wasn’t about pride—it was just practicality.

His knee hurt. His body was cold.

He muttered a curse under his breath and pulled up the conversation.

Is your offer still open?

The response was almost immediate.

˶ᵔ ᵕ ᵔ˶ Always. Where are you? I’ll send a car.

Mydei stared at the message, fingers tightening around his phone. Phainon hadn’t even teased him for it. Hadn’t rubbed it in or made a joke at his expense.

That should’ve made this easier. Instead, it made his chest feel too tight.

With a short sigh, he sent his location and pocketed his phone, tilting his head back to stare at the blurred lights of the city.

This was going to be a long night.

A few minutes passed before a sleek car pulled up beside him, the sound of the engine humming in the rain-soaked quiet. Mydei stood up slowly, his leg protesting the movement. The wet pavement made each step feel more awkward than it had to, but he pushed through, ignoring the pang that shot up his knee with every weight shift. He didn’t want to think about it anymore—just one more thing to add to the list of inconveniences tonight.

He reached the car, tapping on the window. The driver rolled it down, giving him a small nod.

“You Mydei?” the man asked, glancing at him through the rain-dappled glass.

“Yeah,” Mydei replied, pulling the collar of his jacket higher to shield his neck from the cold. He swung open the door and slid into the back seat, trying to avoid putting too much pressure on his leg as he shifted.

The car sped through the streets of New York, the city lights flashing by in a blur. Mydei stared out the window, watching the rain streak down the glass. His thoughts wandered back to the conversation with Phainon—how it had felt strangely normal, despite the distance between them. Despite everything.

He couldn’t remember the last time they had talked like that, casually. The distance, the years of silence, and his stubbornness—it all felt like a distant memory now. He was here, after all. In the same city.

The driver took a turn, and soon enough, the car came to a stop in front of a large building. Mydei rubbed his face, his fingers brushing over the stubble growing on his jaw, and sighed. This was it.

He stepped out and gave the driver a small nod before heading toward the entrance. The lobby was quiet, the lights soft and calming compared to the bustle of the city outside. It felt a little surreal like he didn’t belong in such a place.

The receptionist at the desk smiled warmly when she saw him. “Good evening, sir. Your suite is ready.”

He nodded silently, still processing the whole situation. This wasn’t just a suite. It was Phainon’s suite. Phainon had offered it without a second thought.

After a quick exchange, Mydei grabbed the room key and headed for the elevator. His legs were starting to feel heavy, and the ache in his knee wasn’t letting up. The lift doors closed, and he leaned against the wall as it ascended, staring at his reflection in the mirrored walls, trying to ignore the weight of his thoughts.

When the doors opened, he stepped out into the hallway and made his way to the door Phainon had said would be his. The key turned in the lock with a soft click, and he stepped inside. The suite was quiet, spacious, and almost too nice for someone who was still trying to get used to being there.

Mydei dropped his bag by the door, his body slumping with relief as he let himself relax for the first time that day. He glanced around, taking in the lavish decor, but his mind was too preoccupied to appreciate the space fully.

Phainon had offered this. No strings attached.

Maybe he didn’t have to make everything so complicated. Maybe, for once, he could just breathe.

But when he heard the sound of rain hitting the windows, he felt the tightness in his chest again.

It wasn’t about the offer.

It was about what he might be feeling again.

And that was something he wasn’t sure he was ready to face.

The moment Mydei stepped into the suite, the weight of the day seemed to settle deeper in his bones. The world outside blurred, the sounds of New York just barely registering in the back of his mind as he moved through the expansive space. He felt disconnected like he was walking through someone else’s life—too caught up in his thoughts to take in the luxury of his surroundings.

His hand was on the arm of the chair, ready to drop his bag when—

The bathroom door creaked open.

Mydei froze.

Out of nowhere, Phainon emerged from the bathroom, a towel hanging loosely around his waist, his wet hair dripping dark strands down his neck. For a split second, their eyes met, and Mydei’s heart stuttered. His brain malfunctioned. The sudden sight—Phainon, looking all too effortless, just as gorgeous as he always was but in a completely different way now—sent a jolt through him that he wasn’t prepared for.

Phainon blinked, clearly surprised to see him standing there before his lips curved into a teasing grin.

“You’re here already? Great!” he said casually, as though he hadn’t just walked out of the shower in nothing but a towel.

Mydei’s body seized up. His mind scrambled for words, but everything just turned into static. He could feel his face burning, blood rushing to his ears. What do I do? What the hell do I do?

Before he could even think, his hand jerked forward—slamming the door shut with a thud.

“Put some damn clothes on!” Mydei barked, his voice shaky, his heart hammering in his chest. He didn’t care how loud he sounded. He was dying in embarrassment.

Inside the suite, he stood there for a moment, staring at the door like it was the only thing that could save him from the wave of awkwardness crashing over him. His knee thumped painfully, but he barely noticed the discomfort. Everything else—every ounce of his focus—was consumed by the sheer mortification of the situation. His breath came a little too fast, but he tried to calm himself down, swallowing the lump in his throat.

For a long moment, all he could hear was the sound of his own racing heart.

Then, through the door, Phainon’s laughter echoed, light and carefree. “You’re kidding, right?” His voice was muffled but unmistakably amused. “I’m just trying to make you feel at home. Can’t help that I’m the only one here with decent looks, right?”

Mydei scrubbed a hand over his face. This is going so well, he thought bitterly. I am the worst.

He stood frozen for another moment, trying to catch his breath, but the sounds from behind the door didn’t stop. Phainon’s voice drifted through again, more playful than before, “Just chill out, Mydei. I’ll be done in a second.”

Mydei stared at the door, trying to force his body to move, to escape the awkwardness. It felt like his insides were on fire.

Finally, after what felt like an eternity, the door clicked open again. Phainon stepped into the room, now dressed—casual, loose t-shirt and shorts—his

hair still damp, though now more presentable. He leaned casually against the doorframe, looking completely unbothered by the whole situation. His grin was even bigger now, clearly enjoying Mydei’s discomfort.

“Better?” Phainon asked his tone teasing but not unkind.

Mydei looked at him, fighting the urge to roll his eyes. “Yeah, sure. Whatever,” he muttered, his voice betraying how flustered he still felt. He quickly glanced away, his gaze catching the corner of the room, anywhere but on Phainon, who was enjoying himself too much.

Phainon just chuckled, stepping fully into the room. “Good. I was about to offer you a drink, but now you’re just making me feel awkward. Make yourself comfortable. I’ve got the place to myself, so we can just relax.”

Relax. Mydei almost laughed at the idea of relaxing, but not after that. He still felt like he was trying to recover from the moment he’d walked in here. But there was something in Phainon’s easygoing tone—his usual charm— that made Mydei just nod if only to move past it.

“Right,” he muttered. “Guess I’ll just… sit down then.”

Phainon waved a hand dismissively, heading toward the fridge. “Yeah, go ahead. I’ll get you something to drink. You’ve probably traveled a long way. It’s on me.”

Mydei, still trying to get his bearings, sank into the couch, trying to ignore the strange tension in the air. He tried to focus on anything other than how much his heart was still pounding.

It wasn’t just the sudden vulnerability—seeing Phainon so casually undressed had shaken him more than he realized. It was something deeper, something unspoken between them. And Mydei wasn’t sure he was ready to face it just yet.

The room fell into a silence that felt thick with unacknowledged awkwardness, and Mydei focused on the flickering lights outside, the hum of the city barely filtering through the windows.

Finally, Phainon returned, drink in hand, and handed it over with a grin. “Did you miss New York at all?” he asked, trying to fill the space with something casual. “I mean, I can’t blame you if you didn’t. It’s a bit much.”

Mydei took a drink, his fingers brushing Phainon’s for the briefest second. He blinked, catching his breath. “It’s fine,” he muttered, eyes still flicking around the room. “Still trying to get used to it.”

Phainon didn’t press him, thankfully. Instead, he leaned against the counter, waiting for Mydei to say more—but Mydei didn’t know what else to say. The air felt too heavy now, full of things neither of them could put into words.

For now, Mydei focused on the drink in his hand, trying not to think about the wave of confusion and embarrassment still crashing over him.

Because, for the first time in a while, things between him and Phainon felt a little too real.

The night stretched on in an easy flow of conversation. After the initial awkwardness of the bathroom incident, Phainon and Mydei settled into a more familiar rhythm. The tension had softened, replaced by the kind of casual camaraderie that came with years of friendship—or whatever this was between them now.

They talked about everything and nothing. Phainon teased Mydei about his unwillingness to embrace the chaos of New York, and Mydei rolled his eyes, but there was a comfort in their back-and-forth that settled some of the unease still lingering in Mydei’s chest.

At some point, Phainon pulled up an old movie on the TV, one of those cheesy action flicks that had been a favorite of theirs back when they were younger before everything had become complicated. Mydei barely paid attention to the plot—he didn’t care—but the familiar banter, the explosions, and ridiculous fight scenes felt grounding. It was like they were teenagers again, sitting on a couch, laughing at bad dialogue, and eating junk food.

And maybe that’s what made the night feel easy. Phainon wasn’t forcing anything. He was just here, laughing with Mydei, his usual cocky charm mixing effortlessly with the more relaxed, quieter moments they were sharing.

At some point, Phainon moved to stretch out on the couch, but before he could make himself comfortable, his head flopped over onto Mydei’s shoulder with a soft, hal-asleep chuckle. Mydei didn’t react right away, his mind too slow to register what had just happened. Phainon was warm, his hair still damp and soft against Mydei’s skin. The weight of his head felt both natural and unexpected.

“You’re not that tired, are you?” Mydei teased, his voice a little too quiet, not entirely sure how to react to the sudden proximity. Phainon didn’t reply, but his breathing had already slowed, and he seemed more comfortable than Mydei had seen him in a while.

Mydei shifted slightly, trying not to disturb Phainon, but the sensation of his head resting on him felt oddly intimate, different from their usual banter-filled closeness. There was no teasing, no pretending. Just two people in a room, quietly existing together. Mydei felt his breath even out as the strange knot in his chest loosened.

It wasn’t like he hadn’t spent time with Phainon before—hadn’t shared private moments, even, but this felt different. For the first time in a while, it felt like they were both just… there. No rivalry. No complicated feelings. Just two people, sharing a night without expectations.

Mydei leaned back into the couch, his thoughts swirling, but he didn’t move. He wasn’t sure if he should. He didn’t know how long it would last, this quiet moment where the distance between them was just that—silent, comfortable distance.

But as Phainon continued to sleep, his breathing steady and soft against Mydei’s shoulder, Mydei found himself for once just letting go of the thoughts running through his head. The constant ache in his knee was still there, but in this moment, it almost didn’t matter. He had spent so long keeping his walls up, protecting himself from whatever this thing was

between them. But with Phainon’s head on his shoulder, the walls felt a little less necessary.

He didn’t know how much time passed, but eventually, he felt his eyelids grow heavy, the quiet hum of the city outside lulling him into a drowsy state. For once, Mydei let himself relax, just a little, feeling the warmth of Phainon next to him. It wasn’t the resolution of everything, but it was enough for now.

Eventually, Phainon stirred a little, shifting slightly, but didn’t fully wake. Mydei felt his chest tighten slightly at the thought of Phainon leaving, but for now, he just stayed there, waiting for the next moment, whatever it might bring.

Maybe they didn’t need to talk about all the things that had happened. Maybe tonight could just be… tonight.

And that, strangely enough, was enough. (He keeps telling himself it’s enough, it has to be.)

The morning light filtered softly through the windows, the quiet hum of the city outside barely breaking the stillness in the room. Mydei was the first to wake, his eyes slowly flicking open, the warmth of Phainon’s presence still pressing against him. For a few moments, he just lay there, the early morning light brushing against Phainon’s damp hair, the way it fell in gentle waves around his face. His expression was relaxed, free from the usual tension Mydei saw when Phainon was awake.

It felt strange, at this moment. Mydei had spent years not allowing himself to acknowledge how much he watched Phainon—how much he took in every small detail, every glance, every shift in his posture. But now, with Phainon peacefully asleep beside him, he let himself indulge in it just for a second. The way Phainon’s chest rose and fell in steady rhythm, the soft curve of his lips, the way his brow furrowed slightly even in sleep.

Mydei wasn’t sure how long he lingered like that, but he eventually let out a quiet sigh and shifted, feeling a slight twinge in his knee that reminded him it was still there, still a part of him. His movement caused Phainon to stir

just a little, and for a split second, Mydei thought he might have woken up fully, but Phainon just shifted closer, his head still resting against Mydei’s shoulder.

A small smile tugged at the corner of Mydei’s lips. It was fleeting, but it was there. He didn’t get moments like this often. And in the quiet of the morning, with Phainon so unguarded, Mydei allowed himself to feel it for a moment.

But the peace couldn’t last forever. Eventually, Phainon stirred again, his eyes blinking open, the usual mischievous glint already returning to his gaze as he realized he was still leaning against Mydei.

“Well, good morning,” Phainon said, his voice still a little groggy but warm, the teasing tone creeping in immediately. “Did you enjoy the view, or were you just admiring my stunning good looks?”

Mydei’s smile faded quickly as he shifted away, rolling his eyes and pulling himself up to sit, his tone returning to its usual gruffness. “Get up, you idiot. Practice’s calling.”

Phainon stretched and yawned, the sudden shift back to his usual self making Mydei’s chest tighten just a little. He missed this—the familiar banter, the way Phainon was always so effortlessly confident. It felt almost like the night before had been a dream.

“You’re such a killjoy,” Phainon muttered with a grin, running a hand through his hair. “I was enjoying the quiet, but fine, I’ll go be a responsible adult.”
